# What a healthy diet looks like

> *Patients ask what they should eat, and the useful answer is a dietary pattern built from their own
> food rather than a list of nutrients. We cover the dietary guidelines and plate models, the evidence
> for patterns over single nutrients, and how to apply both to real patients' meals.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain what a dietary guideline is, and distinguish numeric thresholds from plate models such as
  My Healthy Plate.
- Describe the shared core on which My Healthy Plate and the WHO, AHA and US guidelines converge.
- Explain why guidelines lead with dietary patterns instead of single nutrients.
- State the benefit of the Mediterranean (PREDIMED) and DASH trials together with their caveats.
- Explain why popular diets succeed or fail on the energy deficit a person can sustain, and recognise
  when a plan needs a dietitian.
- Adapt My Healthy Plate to a Chinese, Malay or Indian meal, targeting Singapore's wholegrain and
  sodium gaps.
:::

## A healthy diet at a glance {#sec-overview}

In the foundation chapters we took food apart: carbohydrate, fat and protein, vitamins and minerals,
and the gut and metabolism that handle them. Patients eat it whole. The person in front of you does not
eat "45% carbohydrate"; they eat *chicken rice*, *nasi padang* or *thosai* and dhal, and they want to
know whether it is any good.

Needs shift across the life course: folate in pregnancy, calcium and iron in the teens, more protein in
older age (see the *Pregnancy & lactation*, *Childhood & adolescence* and *Healthy ageing* chapters).
Each stage adjusts a shared baseline, the healthy pattern for a general, healthy adult. That
baseline is an archetype: the plate's proportions hold across life stages while the portion and a few
emphases shift, so the pattern is learned once and then adjusted to each patient.

The question becomes answerable once the focus shifts from grading single nutrients to reading the
whole dietary pattern (see the *Why nutrition matters* chapter). Modern guidelines have moved in that
direction, and that shift is why they agree with each other far more than they differ. Reading that
shared pattern and adapting it to a patient's cuisine is the clinician's task. Writing therapeutic meal
plans or prescribing gram targets is a dietitian's work, and knowing where that boundary lies is part
of the clinical skill [@afn2021curriculum].

## Dietary guidelines and plate models {#sec-guidelines}

### What a dietary guideline is {#sec-guideline-def}

A **dietary guideline** is a consensus synthesis: an expert body reads the whole weight of evidence and
translates it into advice a population can act on [@who2020diet; @herforth2019fbdg]. That is its
strength, because it does not rest on any single striking trial, and its limit, because it lags the science
and involves judgement.

Guidelines take two forms: **numeric thresholds** for populations (limits on free sugars, salt,
and saturated and *trans* fat) and **plate models** for individuals (proportions shown on a plate).
Singapore, like most countries, publishes both.

### My Healthy Plate {#sec-plate}

Singapore's patient-facing guide is the Health Promotion Board's My Healthy Plate (introduced in the
*Why nutrition matters* chapter). It is built on one memorable proportion, "quarter, quarter, half":
half the plate fruit and vegetables, a quarter wholegrains and a quarter meat and other
protein, with three companion messages: choose water over sugary drinks, use healthier oils, and stay
active [@hpbHealthyPlate].

The plate leaves out calorie counting, grams and forbidden foods. It is proportional and motivational:
a picture to aim at, with no arithmetic. That is a deliberate design choice for first-line public
messaging. My Healthy Plate dates from 2014 [@hpb2014plate] (the HealthHub page was last reviewed in 2025); it remains current
national guidance.

::: {.callout-note}
## The plate is a proportion, not a portion size
"Quarter, quarter, half" sets the ratio of the plate, not its size. A rugby player and a sedentary retiree can both eat
"quarter, quarter, half"; the amounts differ, the proportions do not. The plate therefore applies equally well
across ages, jobs and cuisines: it fixes the proportions of a meal and leaves the amount to appetite and need.
:::

### Reading an international guideline {#sec-international}

My Healthy Plate closely resembles the major international guidelines. Three are worth knowing for
their structure and intent (the full nutrient targets are in the *Macronutrients* and *Micronutrients,
hydration and electrolytes* chapters):

- The WHO Healthy Diet sets the reference standards: variety; plenty of fruit and
  vegetables; free sugars under 10% of energy (better under 5%); *trans* fat under 1%; salt under 5 g
  a day [@who2020diet].
- The American Heart Association's 2021 guidance (AHA 2021) reframes heart-healthy eating as a pattern
  with ten features: favour vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, legumes, healthy protein sources and liquid
  plant oils; minimise added sugar, salt, alcohol and ultra-processed foods. It explicitly urges
  thinking in patterns, not single nutrients [@aha2021diet].
- The Dietary Guidelines for Americans (US DGA) are federal policy across the whole life course, built
  around a core of vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, varied protein and unsaturated oils, with limits on
  added sugar, saturated fat and sodium [@dga2020].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Guidelines evolve and are debated
Guidance is a moving, contested consensus, not fixed truth. A new 2025–2030 edition of the US
guidelines was released in January 2026 [@dga2025] and drew immediate expert criticism over its handling of
saturated fat and protein. For now, the stable 2020–2025 edition is the reference here. The debate is
itself a live case study in how dietary evidence is argued (see the *Evidence vs hype* chapter).
:::

### Where the guidelines converge {#sec-convergence}

Side by side, the guidelines disagree on very little. A global review of 90 national food-based dietary
guidelines found some messages nearly universal: eat a variety of foods, eat fruit, vegetables and
legumes, and limit sugar, fat and salt [@herforth2019fbdg]. The four guidelines compared here share a
slightly longer list, taken from each guideline's own text [@hpbHealthyPlate; @who2020diet; @aha2021diet; @dga2020]:

| Shared message | My Healthy Plate | WHO | AHA 2021 | US DGA |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Eat a variety of foods | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Plenty of fruit & vegetables | ✓ (½) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Prefer wholegrains | ✓ (¼) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Include legumes / plant proteins | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Limit free/added sugar | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Limit salt | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Prefer unsaturated over saturated/*trans* fat | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Limit ultra-processed foods | not stated | ✓ | ✓ | not stated |

The wording and the pictures differ; the substance is the same short list. When a patient asks "which
diet is right?", the answer is reassuring: the guidelines broadly agree, and the shared advice is
simple. Eat mostly plants and whole foods, and limit sugar, salt and highly processed
products.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: at the same family dinner, a construction worker eats far more than his office-based wife. Why can both plates be on target?
My Healthy Plate fixes the proportions of a meal (half fruit and vegetables, a quarter wholegrains, a
quarter protein), not its size. The amounts differ with appetite and need while the shape stays the
same, so a large plate and a small one are both on target when each keeps those proportions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient has read that WHO, the AHA and the US guidelines all say different things. What follows for the advice you give?
The guidelines differ in wording and pictures, but their substance is the same short list: a review of
90 national food-based guidelines found variety, fruit and vegetables, legumes and limits on sugar,
fat and salt nearly universal, and the major guidelines add wholegrains and unsaturated fat in place
of saturated and *trans* fat. Advice can therefore rest on that shared core, whichever guideline the
patient has read.
:::

## Dietary patterns versus single nutrients {#sec-patterns}

Guidelines increasingly lead with patterns because people eat foods, not nutrients, and foods act in
combination. The idea of **food synergy** holds that a whole dietary pattern can predict health better
than any nutrient studied in isolation [@jacobs2003synergy]. Food synergy is part of why the AHA now
frames its advice as a pattern and warns against chasing single nutrients [@aha2021diet].

::: {.example}
An orange behaves differently from a vitamin-C tablet plus fibre plus sugar.
:::

The pattern view also answers the recurring "is [food] good or bad now?" question. Butter, eggs,
coffee, red meat: asked in isolation, each generates a decade of contradictory headlines. Asked as
"what pattern is this part of?", the findings become more consistent. Asking about one food in isolation is the wrong
question, a trap known as single-nutrient reductionism (see the *Why nutrition matters* chapter).

::: {.callout-note}
## How strong is the case for patterns over single nutrients?
The food-synergy argument is a framework, not a measured effect size: a way of reading evidence, well
supported in principle but not a number to quote. Pattern-level risk reductions often look larger than
single-nutrient ones, but comparing them fairly is itself a subtle appraisal problem. The idea is
sound, but its size is easily overstated.
:::

Two named patterns, Mediterranean and DASH, show the idea at work. Each has a landmark trial, and
each trial's limits should be quoted with its result.

### The Mediterranean pattern {#sec-mediterranean}

**What it is.** A pattern, not a recipe: abundant vegetables, fruit, wholegrains and legumes;
extra-virgin olive oil as the main fat; nuts and fish regularly; modest dairy and poultry; little red
and processed meat.

**The evidence, with its caveats.** The landmark trial is PREDIMED. It randomised higher-risk Spanish
adults to a Mediterranean diet (supplemented with olive oil or nuts) or a control diet, and reported
roughly a 30% relative reduction in a composite of major cardiovascular events [@estruch2018predimed].
A relative reduction is a fall expressed as a share of the starting risk; a composite counts several
outcomes together as one result. Two caveats belong with that main result whenever it is quoted:

- The benefit was stroke-dominated: the composite was driven by fewer strokes, while heart attack and
  cardiovascular death were not individually significantly reduced.
- The original 2013 paper was retracted and re-published in 2018 after randomisation irregularities
  came to light. The reanalysis upheld the main result, and the episode shows that even landmark trials
  get corrected.

Observational data broadly agree: an umbrella review of many meta-analyses links higher Mediterranean
adherence to lower cardiovascular mortality, fewer heart attacks and, most strongly, fewer strokes,
plus less type 2 diabetes [@medUmbrella]. That is a strong evidence base, although much of it is
observational.

Weighing a "30% reduction" of this kind means asking two questions. Is it relative or absolute (the
actual difference in risk between the groups)? And does it count a composite or a hard endpoint (an
outcome that matters to the patient directly, such as a heart attack or death)? Both questions belong to
trial appraisal (see the *Evidence vs hype* chapter).

### The DASH pattern {#sec-dash}

**What it is.** DASH (*Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension*) emphasises fruit, vegetables and
low-fat dairy, with wholegrains, nuts and legumes, and reduced saturated fat and red meat.

**The evidence, with its caveats.** In the original controlled-feeding trial, the DASH diet lowered
blood pressure by about 5.5/3.0 mmHg overall, and by roughly 11.4/5.5 mmHg in participants who were
already hypertensive [@appel1997dash]. Four features of the design determine what that result shows:

- Participants were fed all their food.
- Body weight and sodium were held constant, so the fall came from the pattern itself, not from weight
  loss or salt reduction.
- The endpoint was blood pressure, a surrogate endpoint (a measured marker that stands in for a hard
  endpoint), not heart attacks or strokes.
- The trial ran for only about eight weeks.

The trial clearly shows that a dietary pattern can lower a risk factor; by itself, it is not
proof of long-term event reduction. Cutting sodium on top of DASH lowers blood pressure further. The
therapeutic use of DASH, sodium reduction included, belongs to the *Cardiovascular disease &
hypertension* chapter; the sodium–blood pressure link itself is in the *Micronutrients, hydration and
electrolytes* chapter.

::: {.callout-important}
## The rule for citing any landmark trial
State the benefit and its caveat, together, every time: relative versus absolute risk, surrogate
versus hard endpoint, the population studied, the certainty of the evidence. A benefit quoted without
its caveat overstates the evidence, and spotting the omission is a skill in its own right (see the *Evidence vs
hype* chapter).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient asks whether eggs or coffee are "good or bad" now. What question works better, and why?
Asking what pattern the food is part of. Judged in isolation, each food generates a decade of
contradictory headlines. At the level of the pattern the findings are more consistent, because foods act in
combination and a whole dietary pattern can predict health better than any nutrient studied alone
(food synergy). Food synergy is a framework for reading evidence, though, not an effect size to quote.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: in the DASH trial, body weight and sodium were held constant. Why does that matter, and what can the trial still not show?
Because weight and salt intake did not change, the fall in blood pressure (about 5.5/3.0 mmHg) can be
attributed to the dietary pattern itself, not to weight loss or salt reduction. The endpoint, however,
was blood pressure, a surrogate, measured over about eight weeks in participants who were fed all their
food. The trial therefore shows that a pattern can lower a risk factor, not that it prevents heart attacks
or strokes over the long term.
:::

## Advising real patients {#sec-advising}

### Popular diets: what to tell patients {#sec-popular-diets}

Patients ask about keto, intermittent fasting, paleo or the diet a colleague swears by, not about
"dietary patterns". "Not recommended" is not the same as "not worth knowing": a clinician who cannot
discuss these diets credibly loses the patient's trust. Each can be judged by the same question: is this a
coherent, sustainable way of eating, or a restrictive fad?

When diets are tested head-to-head, the macronutrient split barely matters. A healthy low-fat and a
healthy low-carb diet produced the same ~5–6 kg weight loss over a year, and neither a person's
genotype nor their insulin secretion predicted which diet would suit them [@gardner2018dietfits].
Trials comparing every mix of fat, protein and carbohydrate reach the same conclusion [@sacks2009pounds].
What predicts success is the energy deficit a person can sustain, which comes down to adherence and
food quality. Most popular diets "work" through that same mechanism: a person eats less, of better
food, in a way they can keep up. The table below applies that finding to each popular diet, with
the evidence behind it:

| Diet | What the evidence shows | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Low-carb / ketogenic | Real, fast early weight loss that attenuates after a few months; adherence is hard, LDL cholesterol can rise, and most of the trial evidence is low-certainty [@keto2023umbrella] | A tool, not a cure |
| Intermittent fasting / time-restricted eating | A genuine circadian rationale, but head-to-head trials show it is no better than ordinary calorie restriction [@liu2022tre; @lin2023tre]; it works only for people whom it helps to eat less | A reasonable structure for some, with no special metabolic benefit |
| Paleo, "clean eating" and similar | They usually "work" to the extent that they cut ultra-processed food and added sugar, while excluding whole food groups such as dairy, grains and legumes | The cuts help; the exclusions are unnecessary and risk nutrient gaps |
| Plant-based / vegetarian | The one popular pattern that aligns with the guidelines' plant-predominant message | Healthful when well planned; mind vitamin B12 |

The physiology of fasting and ketosis is in the *Integrative metabolism* chapter, and time-restricted
eating is appraised in the *Evidence vs hype* chapter. Two therapeutic uses in type 2 diabetes are
real but specific, and distinct from each other: a low-carbohydrate pattern, and the low-calorie total diet replacement used for remission (see the *Type 2 diabetes* chapter).

The best diet for a patient is the healthy pattern they will sustain, not the most elaborate one. When a
patient raises a popular diet, dismissing it ends the conversation. Instead, ask what they are hoping
for and find the part worth keeping: if low-carb got them off sugary drinks and refined rice, keep
that. From there, steer toward whichever sustainable pattern fits their life, based on My
Healthy Plate. The main harm to watch for is disordered eating, which restrictive fad diets can
trigger: keep the language weight-neutral, and refer if a red flag appears (see the *Assessing diet and
talking to patients* chapter).

### The food environment: Singapore's national tools {#sec-food-environment}

Knowing the healthy pattern is only half the problem. People choose food inside a **food environment**
(what is sold, priced, labelled and placed within reach), and that environment shapes much of what
they choose. Singapore therefore pairs advice with national tools that reshape the food
environment:

| Tool | Applies to | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Nutri-Grade | Packaged and freshly prepared drinks | Grades each drink A to D by sugar (and saturated fat), shown front-of-pack; the worst grades face advertising limits [@hpbNutriGrade] |
| Healthier Choice Symbol | Packaged products | Flags products that are better within their category, so a shopper can compare at a glance [@hpbHealthierChoice] |
| Healthier Dining Programme | Hawker stalls and restaurants | Marks lower-calorie and wholegrain options where people eat out [@hpbHealthierDining] |

In a randomised trial of the Nutri-Grade label, shoppers bought drinks with less sugar, but the label
alone did not improve the overall quality of their basket: a nudge shifts one choice, not a whole diet
[@nutriGradeRCT2023].

The clinical task at this stage is to recognise that policy and environment shape what people
eat, and to point patients toward these tools. Reading a nutrition label or a Nutri-Grade grade with
a patient is a clinical skill in its own right (see the *Assessing diet and talking to patients*
chapter).

### From guideline to a real plate {#sec-real-plate}

My Healthy Plate is one target, and Singaporeans reach it through three cuisines. The aim is to rebuild
a family's own Chinese, Malay or Indian cooking to the quarter-quarter-half proportions, not to hand the
family a "Mediterranean diet": that pattern is a set of principles to adapt, not a menu to impose.

Build a balanced dinner in each of the three cuisines below. Each household starts on its habitual
plate; swap the slots until all four are on target, and compare how the same target is reached with
entirely different dishes.

<div data-island="healthy-plate" data-src="/diagrams/healthy-plate.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-note}
## 🔬 Food science: why the whole pattern matters
No single swap on that plate accounts for the benefit; the effects are mechanistic and cumulative. Brown rice
in place of white lowers the glycaemic response (the glycaemic-load idea from the *Macronutrients*
chapter), so the post-meal glucose and insulin demand is gentler. The fibre in the wholegrains,
vegetables and legumes then has three effects:

- It slows gastric emptying and blunts the glucose rise.
- It adds bulk that promotes satiety (the fullness after a meal that delays the next one; see the
  *Appetite and weight regulation* chapter).
- What reaches the colon is fermented by gut bacteria into short-chain fatty acids (see *The gut
  microbiome* chapter).

The oily fish adds omega-3 fatty acids, and the vegetable half brings potassium and polyphenols. The
whole assembly (more plants and fibre, less refined starch, better fat, water in place of sugar) is
what the evidence links to better health: food synergy on a plate, which shifts a pattern instead of dosing a
single nutrient [@jacobs2003synergy].
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
Meet the plate's proportions with hawker choices [@hpbHealthyPlate]:

- Ask for more vegetables (a side of stir-fried greens, extra *ulam*, a vegetable *subji*) and a
  smaller rice scoop.
- Choose steamed or grilled over fried (sliced-fish soup, *ikan bakar*, *thosai* with dhal).
- Count dhal, *tau kwa* and legumes as a full protein quarter.
- Default to water or an unsweetened drink over a Nutri-Grade C/D one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍳 Healthy kitchen
At home the plate is easier to follow:

- Cook half the pot as vegetables.
- Switch to brown or mixed rice, or a wholemeal chapati.
- Build meals around fish, tofu, eggs and legumes.
- Keep the cooking oil unsaturated and light.
- Go easy on coconut gravy and ghee.

Small, repeated changes to everyday meals matter more than any occasional "superfood".
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a healthy low-fat and a healthy low-carb diet produced the same weight loss over a year. What follows for a patient who wants to try keto?
The macronutrient split barely matters; what predicts success is the energy deficit a person can
sustain, which comes down to adherence and food quality. The best diet for this patient is the healthy
pattern they will keep up. In practice, you ask what they are hoping for and keep any part of the plan
that helps (dropping sugary drinks and refined rice, for example). You then steer toward a sustainable
pattern based on My Healthy Plate, watch for signs of disordered eating, and refer if a red flag
shows.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a Malay family eats *nasi padang* most nights. Why rebuild that meal to the plate instead of prescribing a Mediterranean diet?
My Healthy Plate fixes the proportions of a meal, not its dishes, so the family's own food can reach
the target. The swaps are more vegetables and *ulam*, a modest rice scoop with less gravy, grilled
*ikan bakar* in place of fried chicken, and water or *teh-o kosong*. The Mediterranean pattern is a
set of principles to adapt, not a menu to impose.
:::

## Is there one best diet? {#sec-close}

No single diet is best. A healthy diet is a pattern that keeps the shared core on which the major
guidelines converge: mostly plants and whole foods, wholegrains in place of refined staples,
unsaturated fats, and little free sugar and salt. Among the patterns that meet it, the best for a
patient is the one they will keep eating, which is usually their own cuisine adapted to the plate's proportions.
When a plan has to become therapeutic or restrictive, it passes to a dietitian [@afn2021curriculum].

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

The emphasis on wholegrains, sugary drinks and salt follows from where Singapore's diet falls short.
The National Nutrition Survey 2022 found that only about 4% of the staples Singaporeans eat are
wholegrain, against the quarter-plate the guideline recommends, and that roughly nine in ten residents
exceed the recommended sodium intake; sugar-sweetened drinks are the single biggest source of dietary sugar, supplying about half of it [@mohNNS2022]. The two main changes are therefore to shift refined rice and noodles toward wholegrains, and to cut the free sugar and salt. The brown-rice swap and the water-over-sugary-drink swap
address these two gaps directly.

The plate's adaptability to each cuisine is also a cultural strength. Singapore's three major
cuisines show one guideline met by three different menus: the plate works at the family table, the
festival spread and the hawker centre because it adapts to each cuisine instead of replacing it. A diet a patient will keep is more useful than a "better" one they soon abandon.
